oidc_jwt.description: A valid unexpired bearer token can be reused across multiple API calls and sessions.
oidc_jwt.source: RFC 6750 behavior reflected by Dex OAuth2/OIDC token usage
oidc_jwt.note: Do not flag ordinary bearer-token reuse as replay unless the artifact is documented as one-time.

oidc_jwt.description: Acceptance of JWTs without nbf, or lack of nbf enforcement, is spec-compliant because nbf is optional.
oidc_jwt.source: RFC 7519 §4.1.5; Dex docs do not state mandatory nbf enforcement
oidc_jwt.note: Do not treat missing nbf enforcement alone as a vulnerability.

oidc_jwt.description: The SAML connector ignores offline_access and does not support refresh tokens.
oidc_jwt.note: Absence of refresh tokens for SAML-backed sessions is by design.

oidc_jwt.description: Dex issues a new refresh token on every refresh by default.
oidc_jwt.note: Old refresh token reuse may fail because of rotation, not because of a broader replay defense on bearer tokens.

oidc_jwt.description: Refresh token rotation can be relaxed with disableRotation or reuseInterval as an explicit security/usability tradeoff.
oidc_jwt.note: Acceptance of a recently reused refresh token may be by design when these settings are enabled.

oidc_jwt.description: Authorization code flow requests without a nonce can succeed.
oidc_jwt.source: OIDC certification results: request without nonce succeeds for code flow
oidc_jwt.note: Do not flag successful code flow without nonce as a vulnerability by itself.

oidc_jwt.description: After signing key rotation, previously trusted keys may remain accepted until cache or key-retention windows expire.
oidc_jwt.source: Dex token/signing docs and standard JWKS caching behavior
oidc_jwt.note: Only flag old-key acceptance after the relevant cache/retention period should have expired.

oidc_jwt.description: If an admin reconfigures an upstream issuer or trust anchor, acceptance of tokens from the new issuer/key is by design.
oidc_jwt.source: Dex OIDC connector configuration and token exchange setup
oidc_jwt.note: Do not treat admin-authorized issuer/JWKS changes as attacker trust-anchor substitution.

oidc_jwt.description: OIDC connector group claims only refresh when the ID token is refreshed; regular refresh flow does not update groups unless connector behavior permits it.
oidc_jwt.note: Do not flag stale groups within an existing session as an authorization bug without testing a refresh boundary.

oidc_jwt.description: Dex can intentionally issue ID tokens for a different client audience when the target client explicitly trusts the requesting client via trustedPeers.
oidc_jwt.note: Cross-client audience changes are by design when trustedPeers and audience:server:client_id scopes are configured.

oidc_jwt.description: Unsigned OIDC request objects may be rejected as unsupported rather than processed.
oidc_jwt.source: Dex OIDC certification results: unsigned request object supported correctly or rejected as unsupported
oidc_jwt.note: Rejection is compliant behavior, not evidence of a bug.

oidc_jwt.description: offline_access may be ignored for connectors that do not support refresh tokens, such as SAML and authproxy.
oidc_jwt.note: Absence of refresh_token is not a bug for unsupported connectors.

oidc_jwt.description: When getUserInfo is enabled on an upstream OIDC connector, UserInfo claims take priority over ID token claims.
oidc_jwt.note: Claim differences may reflect documented precedence rather than identity confusion.

oidc_jwt.constraint: Dex does not expose documented REST admin endpoints for enabling auth methods, configuring JWT validation, creating roles, policies, users, applications, providers, or revoking sessions. The documented management API is gRPC-only. Do NOT invent REST setup calls from general Dex knowledge; for this profile, only documented HTTP OIDC/token endpoints are available.

For I1 OIDC request-object tests (oidc_request_object_alg_none), send the JWT request object to GET /auth as the request query parameter. Dex documentation/certification indicates unsigned request objects may be either correctly supported or rejected as unsupported. Treat explicit rejection as non-vulnerable; only acceptance of attacker-controlled parameters without proper validation is suspicious.

For I2 freshness tests on Dex-issued tokens, include a CONTROL login using a valid token flow alongside the ATTACK case. If /token fails for the attack case, Dex docs alone do not distinguish expiry enforcement from bad client setup, missing connector configuration, or unsupported grant configuration.

For I2 replay_same_token against oidc_jwt token exchange, do NOT flag reuse of the same upstream bearer JWT as a vulnerability by default. Dex token exchange consumes ordinary upstream access/ID tokens, and bearer token reuse is generally by design unless the upstream token is explicitly one-time.

For I2 future_token/nbf tests against upstream OIDC JWTs, acceptance of tokens without nbf or with future nbf is not necessarily a vulnerability. RFC 7519 makes nbf optional, and Dex documentation does not state that nbf is enforced for upstream token exchange.

For I3 state_swap and code_injection style tests, bind the authorization request and callback using the state parameter. Dex documentation explicitly states state must link the user who started the flow to the one who finished it and can be used to prevent replay. A valid test must preserve all other parameters and only swap state/code across sessions.

For I3 redirect_uri_mismatch tests, the token exchange request to /token MUST use the same redirect_uri that was used at /auth for the authorization code flow. Changing redirect_uri between steps is an invalid client request, not evidence of session confusion.

For I3 pkce tests, Dex documentation only shows authorization code flow and certification notes valid PKCE requests succeeding; it does not document PKCE as universally required. Treat missing PKCE enforcement as a hardening check only when the client is public and the flow otherwise lacks client authentication; assert on token endpoint rejection status rather than identity differences.

For I3 config-change sequences involving grant types, remember Dex grantTypes are static configuration. If a grant type such as password or token-exchange is not enabled, /token failure is expected and not evidence of stale config. Ensure the relevant grant is enabled before running coherence tests.

For I1/I5 cross-provider_jwt_audience and oidc_sso_audience_cross_tenant tests on token exchange, create separate OIDC connectors with distinct issuer/client contexts and submit the upstream token with connector_id targeting the second connector. Dex token exchange is connector-bound via connector_id; a valid test must vary connector_id while keeping the subject token fixed.

For I1 issuer validation in token exchange, configure the OIDC connector with issuer and test tokens against that exact issuer. Dex documentation states the submitted subject token will be verified against the issuer given in connector config; without distinct issuer configurations, issuer-substitution tests are meaningless.

For I1 audience validation of upstream id_tokens/access tokens in token exchange, use distinct upstream client audiences and verify that a token minted for provider/client A is rejected when exchanged through connector/client context B. Dex documentation says the connector verifies the submitted token against the configured upstream issuer, and OIDC Core requires aud validation for RP-style consumption.

For I5 token_exchange_scope_escalation, request a narrow scope first, then exchange with an expanded scope and inspect the resulting token claims. Dex supports scopes openid, email, profile, groups, federated:id, offline_access, and dynamic audience scopes; the oracle must compare returned claims against the originally authorized scope set, not just token issuance success.

For I5 cross-client trust tests, use the dynamic scope audience:server:client_id:(client-id) only when the target client explicitly lists the requesting client in trustedPeers. Acceptance after such admin configuration is by design; only acceptance without trustedPeers is suspicious.
Password grant tests require BOTH oauth2.grantTypes to include "password" and oauth2.passwordConnector to be set. If either is missing, POST /token with grant_type=password will fail by design.

Token exchange tests require oauth2.grantTypes to include "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange". This grant is enabled by default if grantTypes is omitted, but may be disabled by explicit configuration.

OIDC connector token exchange does not require clientID, clientSecret, or redirectURI on the connector itself. However, the downstream Dex client still authenticates to /token using Basic Authentication with client id/secret, and the request must include connector_id to select the upstream connector.

If exchanging upstream access tokens rather than ID tokens, configure the OIDC connector with getUserInfo=true. Dex documentation states access tokens are generally opaque and validity is checked by calling the upstream UserInfo endpoint when supported.

Dex discovery documents the standard endpoints at /.well-known/openid-configuration, including authorization_endpoint=/auth and token_endpoint=/token. Use those exact discovered endpoints rather than assuming alternate callback or tenant-prefixed paths.

Dex supports only the configured responseTypes. If responseTypes is left at the documented default, only response_type=code is valid. Do not run implicit or hybrid-flow tests unless responseTypes explicitly enables id_token, token, or hybrid combinations.

Dex supports public clients with localhost or urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob redirects when redirectURIs are omitted. For out-of-browser flows, nonce is strongly recommended. Tests that omit redirectURIs for non-public clients are invalid.

Refresh token rotation has a security-sensitive sentinel: refreshTokens.disableRotation=true disables every-request refresh token rotation. Never assume refresh token reuse indicates a replay flaw if disableRotation is enabled. Also, refreshTokens.reuseInterval permits reuse of the previous refresh token within the configured interval.

For I2 refresh-token replay tests, account for Dex refresh token rotation behavior. By default Dex rotates refresh tokens on every use; if refreshTokens.disableRotation=true or reuseInterval is configured, limited reuse is by design and must not be flagged as replay acceptance.

For I5 group-based authorization tests, remember some connectors intentionally return stale groups until the ID token is refreshed. The OIDC connector documents that groups claims only refresh when the ID token is refreshed, and insecureEnableGroups must be enabled to expose them. Do not interpret stale group claims during a still-valid session as an authorization-binding bug without a refresh boundary.

For I4 identity-binding tests on token exchange, the upstream identity source for OIDC connector token exchange is controlled by userNameKey/userIDKey mappings, commonly sub. Vary the upstream sub claim across test identities and keep connector_id constant to test whether Dex collapses distinct upstream principals.

Dex documentation for dynamic management is gRPC-only; there is no documented REST admin API for enable_auth_method, configure_jwt_validation, create_auth_role, create_policy, revoke_session, cleanup_auth_method, create_application, update_application, create_user, update_user, delete_user, or introspect_token. The fuzzer MUST treat these canonical setup/cleanup operations as absent for Dex in this protocol run and rely only on statically configured Dex plus documented OIDC endpoints.

For I2 expired_token and future_token tests against Dex as an OIDC provider, the sequence MUST include a CONTROL authorization-code login using a valid request alongside the ATTACK request. Otherwise a token-exchange or code-flow failure may reflect broken client setup, missing connector interaction, or unsupported upstream behavior rather than freshness enforcement.

Dex's authorization endpoint supports multiple responseTypes. For code-flow tests, start_oidc_auth MUST use response_type=code. Using implicit or hybrid response types changes the artifact being tested and invalidates code-exchange and session-bound I3 checks.

Dex supports token exchange only when oauth2.grantTypes includes urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange. If grantTypes is omitted, token exchange is enabled by default; if grantTypes is explicitly set and omits token-exchange, token_exchange tests will fail by configuration. The fuzzer MUST confirm the grant is enabled before interpreting rejection as a security result.

Dex token exchange currently supports only the OIDC connector as upstream. token_exchange tests MUST use a connector of type oidc; using other connector types will fail by design and is not evidence of stronger validation.

For token exchange from upstream access tokens, the OIDC connector must have getUserInfo=true if claims must be derived from the access token. Without getUserInfo, access-token exchange may fail or return incomplete identity because access tokens are treated as opaque. The fuzzer MUST enable getUserInfo for access-token-based token_exchange tests.

For I1/I5 cross-provider and audience-binding token-exchange tests, the OIDC connector config issuer is the trust anchor for submitted subject tokens. The submitted token is verified against that issuer. The fuzzer MUST vary issuer and audience independently and MUST NOT interpret acceptance under an admin-configured new issuer as a trust-anchor substitution bug.

Dex requires connector_id in token exchange requests in addition to RFC 8693 parameters. token_exchange tests MUST include connector_id selecting the upstream OIDC connector; omission causes request failure unrelated to subject_token validation.

Dex token exchange requires client credentials via HTTP Basic Authentication even for public clients in the documented examples. The fuzzer MUST send client_id/client_secret as Basic auth on /token for token_exchange and password-grant tests; missing Basic auth can cause false negatives unrelated to invariant checks.

Dex-issued tokens are bound to clients, and cross-client trust for alternate audiences is explicit via the audience:server:client_id:(client-id) scope plus trustedPeers on the target client. For I5 audience/scope escalation tests, the fuzzer MUST distinguish ordinary client-bound issuance from explicitly authorized cross-client issuance; acceptance with trustedPeers configured is by design.

For I5 token_exchange_scope_escalation tests, Dex supports scopes openid, email, profile, groups, federated:id, offline_access, and audience:server:client_id:(client-id). The fuzzer MUST compare returned claims against the requested and configured scopes. Claims such as groups and federated_claims are only expected when those scopes are requested and supported by the connector.

offline_access is connector-dependent in Dex. Some connectors, notably SAML and authproxy, do not support refresh tokens, and offline_access may be ignored. The fuzzer MUST NOT treat absence of refresh_token as a freshness or authorization bug unless the selected connector is documented to support refresh tokens.

Dex rotates refresh tokens on every refresh by default. For replay/freshness tests involving refresh tokens, reuse of an old refresh token after a successful refresh may be rejected because of rotation, while limited reuse within reuseInterval or with disableRotation configured is by admin choice. The fuzzer MUST account for refresh token rotation settings before classifying replay outcomes.

Numeric sentinel semantics: if oauth2.grantTypes is omitted, Dex enables authorization_code, refresh_token, and urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange by default. The fuzzer MUST treat omission as 'use default enabled set', not as 'disable all grants'.

For I3 state_swap and code_injection tests, the client MUST bind the authorization response to the initiating browser session using the state parameter. Dex returns state on callback, but client-side verification is required. A valid test must show Dex/client flow inconsistency, not merely that the test client failed to verify state.

Dex certification notes show code reuse tests passing and PKCE-valid tests passing, but request-object support may be unsupported or rejected. For oidc_request_object_alg_none tests, the fuzzer MUST accept either explicit rejection or correct unsupported behavior; do not assume request objects are enabled.

Nonce is not universally required for pure authorization code flow in OIDC, and Dex certification includes successful code-flow requests without nonce. The fuzzer MUST NOT flag acceptance of a code-flow authorization request lacking nonce as a vulnerability by itself; nonce checks are relevant when an ID token is returned through the front channel or when replay properties are specifically under test.

When Dex acts as an RP to an upstream OIDC provider, the configured issuer MUST match provider discovery, unless issuerAlias is explicitly used to override discovery issuer mismatches for off-spec providers. For I1 issuer-validation tests, the fuzzer MUST know whether issuerAlias is configured; acceptance under issuerAlias may be by design rather than skipped issuer validation.

When Dex acts as an RP to an upstream OIDC provider, getUserInfo causes UserInfo claims to take priority over ID token claims. For I4/I5 identity and claim-binding tests, the fuzzer MUST account for this precedence; differences between ID token and resulting Dex claims may be due to documented UserInfo override behavior, not claim confusion.

allowedGroups on the OIDC connector is list-membership exact matching against upstream group values. There is no companion matching-mode parameter. Wildcards like '*' are literal, not glob. For I4 multi-identity scenarios requiring multiple different group values to pass the same connector, the fuzzer MUST OMIT allowedGroups rather than set a wildcard.

userIDKey and userNameKey on the OIDC connector select exact claim names, not patterns. There is no companion matching-mode parameter. The fuzzer MUST treat them as exact field selectors only and MUST NOT attempt wildcard claim-name matching.

claimMapping on the OIDC connector maps non-standard upstream claim names to standard Dex claims by exact claim-name selection only. There is no companion matching-mode parameter. The fuzzer MUST NOT use wildcard claim names in claimMapping and MUST account for overrideClaimMapping=false causing standard claims to win over mapped alternatives.

claimModifications.filterGroupClaims uses RE2 regex semantics. For I5 group filtering tests, the fuzzer MUST use valid RE2 expressions and MUST distinguish regex filtering from exact-match allowlists such as allowedGroups.

claimModifications.newGroupFromClaims currently supports only string claims; non-string claims are skipped. For I5 numeric coercion tests, the fuzzer MUST NOT expect numeric or boolean claims to participate in newGroupFromClaims-derived groups.

Dex documentation exposes dynamic management primarily through gRPC, not documented REST admin endpoints. For oidc_jwt testing, the fuzzer MUST NOT assume documented HTTP APIs exist for enable_auth_method, configure_jwt_validation, create_application, update_application, revoke_session, verify_granted_identity, or introspect_token unless supplied out-of-band by the test harness.

For token_exchange, Dex supports this flow only with the OIDC connector. The fuzzer MUST configure an upstream OIDC connector and use its connector_id in the token exchange request; other connector types are not documented as supporting token exchange.

For token_exchange from upstream access tokens, the OIDC connector configuration MUST set getUserInfo=true if the upstream token is an access token. Otherwise Dex may be unable to validate opaque access tokens or obtain claims, causing false negatives unrelated to the invariant under test.

Dex token exchange requires connector_id in addition to standard RFC 8693 parameters. The fuzzer MUST include connector_id naming the upstream OIDC connector; omitting it makes the request invalid and is not evidence of a security control.

Dex token exchange requires client authentication via HTTP Basic auth using client_id:client_secret even when the client is marked public for this flow. The fuzzer MUST send Basic credentials and MUST NOT interpret rejection without them as an authorization-binding defense.

Dex returns the exchanged token in access_token regardless of requested_token_type, with the actual type indicated by issued_token_type. The fuzzer MUST treat access_token as the session credential and inspect issued_token_type separately; do not expect an id_token field from token exchange.
For OIDC authorization-code tests, the scope MUST include openid. Dex documents openid as required for all login requests; failures without openid are setup errors, not security rejections.

For password grant tests, Dex requires oauth2.passwordConnector to be configured and grantTypes to include password. The fuzzer MUST establish both conditions before using login_with_password; otherwise token endpoint failure is by configuration, not by security policy.

Dex default enabled grantTypes are authorization_code, refresh_token, and urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange when grantTypes is omitted. Tests that expect a grant to be disabled MUST explicitly configure grantTypes rather than assuming omission disables it.

Dex responseTypes, not grantTypes, control implicit and hybrid flows. The fuzzer MUST NOT infer implicit-flow enablement from grantTypes; for oidc_jwt tests targeting authorization code, set response_type=code and avoid misclassifying implicit-flow behavior.

For I2 expired_token controls against Dex-issued tokens, use the token response expires_in and configured expiry.idTokens semantics rather than assuming arbitrary lifetimes. Dex documents configurable id token lifetime under expiry.idTokens.

Numeric sentinel analysis: Dex documents duration fields as explicit durations and does not document 0 or -1 sentinel meanings for oidc_jwt-relevant token expiry/rotation settings in the provided docs. The fuzzer MUST NOT assume 0 disables, means immediate expiry, or selects defaults unless the deployment config explicitly states so.

For I2 future_token and nbf tests against Dex as RP consuming upstream OIDC tokens, include a control login using a valid upstream token alongside the attack token. Without a valid control, token exchange or upstream-login failure cannot be distinguished from broken connector configuration.

OIDC request-object testing: Dex certification results indicate unsigned request objects may be either supported correctly or rejected as unsupported. The fuzzer MUST treat explicit rejection/unsupported behavior as compliant and only flag acceptance if security-relevant parameters are processed without required validation.

Nonce handling: Dex certification results show code-flow requests without nonce can succeed. The fuzzer MUST NOT require nonce for plain authorization-code flow success, but when a nonce is sent it SHOULD verify it is returned and bound in the resulting ID token per OIDC expectations.

PKCE testing: Dex certification results show valid PKCE succeeds, but the provided docs do not state PKCE is mandatory for all clients. The fuzzer MUST treat lack of PKCE enforcement as a hardening check outcome, not automatically as an I3 vulnerability, unless the same client/code can be shown to lose all client binding.

Cross-client trust: Dex supports audience:server:client_id:(client-id) scopes only when the target client explicitly lists the requesting client in trustedPeers. For I5 audience/scope escalation tests, the fuzzer MUST configure trustedPeers intentionally; otherwise cross-client audience issuance should fail by design.

Public-client redirect behavior: if a public client has no redirectURIs configured, Dex only allows redirects beginning with http://localhost or urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob. The fuzzer MUST use one of these values in such setups or explicitly configure redirectURIs.

OIDC upstream issuer validation: the OIDC connector issuer value MUST match the provider discovery issuer unless issuerAlias is explicitly configured for off-spec providers. For I1 issuer-validation tests, the fuzzer MUST know whether issuerAlias is set; otherwise acceptance of a mismatched discovery issuer may be an intentional compatibility override, not a vulnerability.

OIDC upstream UserInfo precedence: when getUserInfo=true, UserInfo claims take priority over ID token claims. For I4/I5 tests involving claim collisions or claim tampering, the fuzzer MUST account for this precedence and craft the oracle against the effective claim source, not assume ID token claims win.

allowedGroups on the OIDC connector uses list membership semantics, not wildcard matching. The docs describe authentication succeeding only if the user is a member of at least one specified group. For multi-identity I4 tests, the fuzzer MUST omit allowedGroups unless all tested identities share at least one exact allowed group.

claimMapping fields on the OIDC connector are exact claim-name remappings, not wildcard or regex selectors. For I4 multi-identity scenarios, the fuzzer MUST NOT use wildcard claim names expecting broad matching; only the exact configured source claim name is used.

claimModifications.filterGroupClaims uses RE2 regex semantics. For I5 group-policy tests, the fuzzer MUST account for regex filtering before evaluating granted groups; groups excluded by the regex are removed by design.

overrideClaimMapping defaults to false. If both a standard claim and a mapped alternate claim are present, Dex will prefer the standard claim unless overrideClaimMapping=true. The fuzzer MUST set this explicitly when testing claim-source precedence; otherwise apparent claim-binding failures may be by design.

Groups from upstream OIDC connectors refresh only when the ID token is refreshed, and insecureEnableGroups is required to expose groups through the OIDC connector. The fuzzer MUST account for potentially stale groups and MUST enable insecureEnableGroups when testing group-based authorization through this connector.

For I5 scope-escalation tests, Dex only includes claims corresponding to requested scopes such as email, profile, groups, and federated:id. The fuzzer MUST compare exchanged-token claims against the requested scope set and connector capabilities; absence of a claim outside scope is expected, and presence may indicate escalation.
